Wow talk about cherry picking data to reach an unjustified conclusion. The article points out that the national rate of drug use is 9.4%. Then it tells us that the states at issue tested 2826 welfare users who answered questionnaires indicating a reasonable suspicion of drug use. Of those, the article claims that "just" 369 of those 2826 returned positive results. What's interesting is that 369 divided by 2826 is actually over 13%, or almost 1.4 times the estimated rate of the national average. Now, without diving deeper into these questionnaires and what qualifies as reasonable suspicion, it's really impossible to estimate how the rate of drug use among those who gave the right answers to avoid testing compares with those who gave answers that resulted in their being tested. It's a known fact that self-reported drug use is widely underreported even in anonymous surveys, and if people know that their welfare is contingent on giving the right answers they're all the more likely to lie. Furthermore, just because someone tests negative, that is not proof positive that they've never used drugs, it just means they haven't used within the window that the test is effective for.

The only fair interpretation of the data here is that, of those tested, there was a 1.4X higher rate of positive test than we would expect from a random sample of the population. While that can't be effectively extrapolated to welfare recipients as a whole, due to selection bias resulting from the questionnaire, it certainly doesn't support the proposition that the 13% who were tested are the only welfare recipients who would test positive if tested, which is what the article is trying to use the data to support.
